first_impression: Clean, confident deck. Real recording, real numbers, honest caveats. Finally someone showing a product instead of a vision.
confusing: Slide 6 header label has overlapping garbled text ('GENERATED / YOU WRITE')
Slide 11 leads with 90x then spends half the slide walling it off with caveats, three speedup numbers (90x, 21x, 4x)
Slide 15 says sim-to-sim DONE but also lists policy-transfer to MuJoCo as next
doubts: Target user is RL students, but 2D planar sims may not match any course assignment
Playground and docs are claimed, but I only saw screenshots; no evidence anyone besides the author has run it
Are classes really blocked on cloud GPU? MuJoCo CPU already runs on MacBooks
questions: Which RL course or club would adopt this next week, and what do they use today?
Can I pip install and train in a minute on a clean M1 Air, not your M3 Pro?
How does this fit alongside Gymnasium and MuJoCo MJX users already have?

fixes.change: Lead with one honest headline (21x vs MuJoCo on all cores, or 295K end-to-end training steps/s). Move the 90x same-solver figure to a footnote.
Add proof of a real user or test: a classmate or club member running the 3 commands on their own MacBook, with a timing and photo.
Fix the overlapping header text and cut the code excerpt to the 5 lines that matter.
Reword 'Sim-to-sim: done' to 'Physics validated vs MuJoCo' so it does not contradict the pending policy-transfer check.

first_impression: Unusually rigorous for a 12-hour build: seeds, error bars, MuJoCo comparison, and a self-caught reward-hacking story. Scope of validation is thin.
confusing: Slide 8 chart reports 54.9 m average episode distance but the replay lanes say 21.5 m in 8 s; the metrics differ and the slide only explains it in fine print
Slide 7 says 494K steps/s with PPO, slide 11 says 295K end-to-end; the two figures are never reconciled
Slide 11: '4x GPU, ~30x kernel fusion' decomposition has no shown measurement
doubts: Physics validation covers a single pendulum, a friction slide and a drop. No contact-rich multi-body gait check, which is where the cheating happened
'Same solver on CPU' baseline may be an unoptimized step-by-step Python or NumPy loop, which makes 90x a strawman
5 seeds with a >10 m threshold is a low bar and is not a controlled comparison; no baseline algorithm or ablation
The cheating fix is shown only via before/after speed and slip; no ablation of warm-starting vs motor curve
questions: What is the CPU baseline implemented in, and is it compiled and multithreaded?
What are the reward function, observation space and PPO hyperparameters? Is the 54.9 m figure reproducible from the repo?
Can you ablate warm-start vs the DC motor curve to show which one removed the slip?
What is the foot-slip metric definition and why is 0.053 m/s acceptable?

fixes.change: Add a contact-rich validation: the same 2-link hopper dropped and driven with fixed torques in both MacGym and MuJoCo, with trajectory RMS error and a contact-force comparison.
State the CPU baseline's language, threading and compilation. Add a compiled multithreaded CPU baseline so the 90x number survives scrutiny.
Add the ablation as a small 2x2 grid (warm-start on/off x motor curve on/off) showing speed and slip for each.
Plot one metric on both chart and lanes (per-episode distance on identical 8 s episodes) and put the definition on-slide, not in fine print.

first_impression: Cute JAX-metal-is-dead pitch, but 2D planar sim is a toy next to MJX and Warp. Honest caveats help, though.
confusing: Slide 11 'same physics' CPU vs GPU is a baseline I don't trust, and 21x vs MuJoCo is admittedly not the same physics
Slide 2 says Mac RL sim is dead, but MuJoCo and MJX-on-CPU run on Mac; the claim only holds for GPU-fast paths
Slide 15 'Sim-to-sim: done' while policy transfer to MuJoCo is still next
doubts: Walker reaching 21.5 m in 8 s from a one-minute run with PPO in 2D says little; planar locomotion is easy and the solver may be forgiving
Pendulum/friction/drop tests don't prove a contact solver is accurate for legged locomotion; the original cheating shows the contact model was exploitable
PPO update is 72% of an iteration, so the sim speed advantage is mostly irrelevant to end-to-end training
Comparing against a community port at 5.2K steps/s on an M3 Max is not a comparable benchmark
questions: Does a policy trained in MacGym transfer to MuJoCo at all? That is the only validation I care about.
How many MuJoCo-Warp-class features does it lack: friction cones, soft contacts, 3D, domain randomization?
What does the observation and reward look like, and how sensitive is learning to the 0.02 s dt with 8 substeps?
Why 4,096 envs as the headline? What is the scaling curve versus env count?

fixes.change: Run the policy-transfer check (train in MacGym, roll out in MuJoCo with matched model) and show the result, even if it fails. A measured gap would be more credible than 'next'.
Replace the headline with the fair_bench scaling curve (steps/s vs env count) plus end-to-end PPO throughput, and drop 90x as the hero number.
Add a validation on the walker itself: same torque sequence in MacGym and MuJoCo and overlay the torso x trajectory.
Narrow the claim to 'no fast GPU path on Mac' and acknowledge MuJoCo CPU and MJX exist, so the problem statement can't be dismissed.

first_impression: Metal-kernel codegen plus real recordings and a reward-hacking post-mortem. Strong for solo and 12 hours, if the numbers hold up.
confusing: Slide 7's 3.2 days of experience is robots x steps x dt, a flashy unit with no scientific meaning
Slide 6 header text collides and the kernel excerpt is truncated with '...', so I can't judge the codegen
Slide 8 chart shows 5/5 seeds at 54.9 m while the replay shows 21.5 m, a metric mismatch
doubts: One GPU thread per robot with a fused kernel is standard; the novelty is the Python-to-Metal compile step, which needs a clearer demo
Foot slip of 0.053 m/s after the fix still exists; contact is a soft impulse approximation, so locomotion gaits may exploit it elsewhere
Built with AI agents in 3 hours of commits (8 commits total); how much did you actually design?
Tests: 18 checks, mostly API and parity, not physics-correctness tests beyond the MuJoCo comparison
questions: How does the compiler handle arbitrary robot topologies; what happens with 20 bodies, or loops?
What is the constraint solver (PGS iterations? 4 per substep?) and how does solution quality scale with iterations?
Why is the PPO update 72% of an iteration on an MLX GPU; is it memory-bound or launch-bound?
Have you seen reward hacking recur after the fix, for example the walker exploiting joint limits?

fixes.change: Show the real codegen on the slide: one generated kernel for the 2-line robot, with an arrow from the joint line to the corresponding torque and impulse lines.
Add a multi-contact validation (a box dropped and slid in MacGym vs MuJoCo, or a 2-link falling onto the ground) with trajectory RMS error.
Replace '3.2 days of experience' as the hero with the clearer 'a minute of training equals X hours of robot time', and one honest line on sample efficiency vs a CPU baseline.
Add the speed-vs-slip plot across training runs before and after the fix so the cheating is shown as a measurable diagnostic, not an anecdote.
